content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method named Global Spatial Correlation Attention (GSCA). As summarized by the paper, GSCA serves as a simple attention module like SENet. The proposed GSCA does not have additional parameters. It has a complexity linear to the number of pixels. In more details, GSCA uses a global average pooling layer to get a global feature. This global feature is used as the key, and each pixel considered as the query gets a pixel-level sigmoid response with the key. This response is reversed and multiplied back with the original pixel features. Following recent works, GSCA also proposes to use a multi-head solution on the channels. GSCA is mostly tested with the ResNet family on ImageNet classification and COCO object detection / instance segmentation. Compared to SE-like methods, the proposed method shows performance improvements.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper proposes a SE-like method for the ResNet family mostly but without introducing any additional parameters. The computation is also kept low due to the global feature computation.

The mutli-head solution also fits nicely with the global spatial correlation attention design. It also seems to bring reasonable improvements to the system.

But as the paper says, the proposed method is designed for convolutional neural networks. With the recent trend of applying vision transformers to more vision tasks, the applicability of the proposed method to more recent works will become questionable.

The intuition of having a global feature attending the pixel features is quite common for vision transformers based solutions, especially for object detection, instance segmentation, etc. But they do have heavy parameters modeling the attention. I think one of the paper’s merits is not using additional parameters.

Having `reverse` in the equation is slightly against intuitions. It’s even more against intuitions to see the performance is a lot worse than baseline without `reverse`. Table 2(b) also shows concerning results where the accuracy is sensitive to alpha and has multiple peaks. I think it would strengthen the paper if the authors include more intuitive discussions about `reverse` and intuitively why it is necessary in the system.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, the paper is clearly written and the quality meets the conference standard. The novelty is reasonable for methods in its family, and the reproducibility looks ok.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method is a SE-like method but without additional parameters. The method is very simple but the results look solid.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Responses to Official Review by Reviewer ahYw
content.comment:
Thank you so much for the detailed and constructive comments. Please see our below responses to your questions one by one.

**To your comment** “But as the paper says, the proposed method is designed for convolutional neural networks. With the recent trend of applying vision transformers to more vision tasks, the applicability of the proposed method to more recent works will become questionable.”

**Our responses** are: We understand your concerns. In this paper, we propose a lightweight self-attention module and demonstrate its effectiveness by combining it with convolution. Indeed, as you say, vision transformers are becoming the trend for more visual tasks. Moreover, the hybrid architectures of convolution and self-attention are also widely studied nowadays. As mentioned in the conclusion, replacing traditional self-attention with GSCA to build a lightweight Conv-Transformer hybrid architecture network and utilizing it with practical deployment is an important part of our future research.

**To your comment** “Having reverse in the equation is slightly against intuitions. It’s even more against intuitions to see the performance is a lot worse than baseline without reverse. Table 2(b) also shows concerning results where the accuracy is sensitive to alpha and has multiple peaks. I think it would strengthen the paper if the authors include more intuitive discussions about reverse and intuitively why it is necessary in the system.”

**Our responses** are: Thank you for such constructive suggestions, this is indeed a critical issue. We have analyzed the reasons for the reverse operation in the revision **Appendix A.6**.

The key matrix $K$ of self-attention is obtained by linear projection, while GSCA gets the key vector $k$ by the feature map's global average pooling (GAP). It causes GSCA to work differently than the intuition that comes from self-attention. Specifically, GAP is challenging to capture the complex information in the feature maps and misses most of the detailed features[1]. In contrast to the general features in the global scope represented by GAP, we believe that spatial attention should enhance special features, such as texture details. Intuitively, enhancing special detail features is helpful for visual recognition tasks. Therefore, we use the reverse operation to enhance the specificity features rather than features similar to the $k$ vector generated by GAP.

To intuitively discuss the necessity of the reverse operation in the system, the feature map of GSCA module is visualized in Figure 5. In short, as the network is optimized iteratively, the reverse operation does not affect the input of GSCA. For the attention weight, the reverse operation drives GSCA to focus almost on the object itself, while GSCA without reverse focuses almost exclusively on the background region. Naturally, the final outputs show that the GSCA without reverse tends to focus on the background. The reversed GSCA drives the network to focus on the object, which is more beneficial for image classification tasks.

[1] Zequn Qin, Pengyi Zhang, Fei Wu, and Xi Li. Fcanet: Frequency channel attention networks. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), pp. 783–792, 2021.

content.title: Responses to Official Review by Reviewer 287a
content.comment:
Thank you so much for the detailed and constructive comments. Please see our below responses to your questions one by one.

**1. To your comment** “My main concern is that GSCA is a simplified self-attention mechanism, where many existing lightweight attention works weaken the contribution. Compared to SOTA, the performance boost from the GSCA is subtle. The best performances of those three vision tasks are still given by the existing work FcaNet. The work is presented more like a technical report, which does not fit ICLR.”

**Our responses** are: We understand your concern about the best performance in the three vision tasks given by FcaNet. However, the competitiveness of GSCA is that it achieves a better tradeoff in accuracy-parameter and accuracy-inference speed. Compared to FcaNet, the superiority of GSCA is summarized as follows. 

(1) **GSCA is lighter than FcaNet.** As shown in Table 4, FcaNet increases 2.5M, 4.7M and 6.5M parameters sequentially as Resnet50 to 152. While GSCA can remain parameter-free.

(2) **GSCA has a higher inference speed than FcaNet.** As shown in Table 4, GSCA consistently maintains a higher inference speed than FcaNet. Moreover, the accuracy gap between GSCA and FcaNet gradually shrinks as the baseline performance is enhanced (only a 0.03% difference between GSCA-152 and FcaNet-152).

(3) **Comparison under the same parameters** GSCA, as a spatial attention module, can be easily combined with SE and ECA to improve the original methods. Tables 5 and 6 show that GSCA achieves equal or similar performance to FcaNet with fewer parameters. With equal parameters, GSCA-SENet outperforms FcaNet in object detection and instance segmentation tasks.

**2. To your comment** “Although GSCA reduces the complexity of self-attention, the works address it in a more technical way, lacking the mathematical proof to explain the insight.”

**Our responses are:** Thank you for your constructive comments. We analyze the computational complexity of traditional self-attention and GSCA in **Appendix A.5** of the revised version. It is illustrated that compared with self-attention, GSCA has linear complexity for the number of pixels. 

**3. To your comment** “Using the Grad-CAM visualization to explain the GSCA’s effectiveness in image classification is questionable. Does a heatmap covering a larger area mean better classification? Regarding classification, it is more about attending to the discriminative parts than covering large areas.”

**Our responses** are: We agree with you that the effectiveness of simply covering a larger area of the heat map for explaining image classification tasks is indeed questionable. However, GSCA does not enhance image classification performance by arbitrarily expanding the heat map area. In Figure 3, we clearly see that the expanded heat map range of GSCA is targeted and mainly covers the recognized object regions (the discriminative parts, as you said). This indicates that GSCA can motivate the model to focus on more feature details of the recognized objects, to better utilize the information in the target object regions and to aggregate features from them, which is beneficial for image classification [1]. Specifically, in Figure 3, for the first two rows of dense or multi-target objects, GSCA can analyze more features from multiple individuals for recognition. Furthermore, facing a single object like the third row, GSCA can focus on more feature details in the recognized object region.
Perhaps the unclear explanation in section 3.3 led to this misunderstanding, and we apologize and have revised the description in the revision.

**4. To your comment** “The paper writing is of poor quality and needs polishing. And some claims/sentences are subjective and lack evidence to support, e.g., all of which is ine…”

**Our responses** are: Thank you for your advice, we have made meticulous modifications to this manuscript. Specifically, we have revised and polished subjective expressions and ambiguous sentences so that readers can understand our work more clearly.

[1] Sanghyun Woo, Jongchan Park, Joon-Young Lee, and In So Kweon. Cbam: Convolutional block attention module. In Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), pp.3–19, 2018.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new attention approximation module dubbed Global Spatial Correlation Attention (GSCA). Combining self-attention and convolution is problematic due to self-quadratic computational cost. In contrast to self-attention, their GSCA employs a single key to make the computational complexity linear, hence resolving the issue. In addition, the proposed approach requires no additional parameters, which is another advantage. The authors demonstrate that GSCA performs well on image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
The GSCA is a new architectural design. In contrast to prior work, they employ cross-correlation operation (Formula 3) and give greater weight to the spatial components that are least connected (Formula 4).
GCSA solves the quadratic computational complexity problem in self-attention in an efficient manner. 
The proposed method can be applied to diverse CNN backbone designs without requiring a great deal of additional computing resources (Table 4).
  
Weaknesses
For their architecture design, sufficient experimental should be performed. In particular, they present no theoretical or empirical justification for replacing cosine-similarity with cross-correlation, which is more commonly utilized in computing attention. They just mention it by saying “GSCA uses the cross-correlation coefficient to evaluate the similarity between each location in query Q and key k.” It might sound better to offer an explanation for this.
In the ImageNet-1k experiment part, authors does not demonstrate a significant improvement in top-1 accuracy when compared to other methods (Table 4). 


--- after rebuttal ---
The authors performed additional experiments related to cross-correlation. However, it is still difficult to say that the performance is better than SOTA methods sufficiently. Therefore, I keep my score.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper offers the information necessary to reproduce their experimental results.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents the attention approximation module known as Global Spatial Correlation Attention (GSCA). This paper demonstrates that the GSCA enhance the performance of several baseline models in classification, detection, and segmentation tasks while using little processing resources. However, they lack sufficient experimental evidence for their architecture (i.e using cross-correlation). In addition, a comparative study of alternative attention approaches (Table 4) diminishes the persuasiveness of the proposed method.

content.title: Responses to Official Review by Reviewer gy9w
content.comment:
Thank you so much for the detailed and constructive comments. Please see our below responses to your questions one by one.

**1. To your comment regarding cosine-similarity and cross-correlation** “For their architecture design, sufficient experimental should be performed. In particular, they present no theoretical or empirical justification for replacing cosine-similarity with cross-correlation, which is more commonly utilized in computing attention. They just mention it by saying “GSCA uses the cross-correlation coefficient to evaluate the similarity between each location in query Q and key k.” It might sound better to offer an explanation for this.”

**Our responses** are: Yes, cosine-similarity is more commonly used to calculate attention scores. In fact, the cross-correlation coefficient can be regarded as the centralized adjusted form of the cosine-similarity, so both are similar in principle. However, the cross-correlation coefficient is less sensitive to the input data compared with the cosine-similarity. We discuss the cross-correlation coefficient and the cosine-similarity in **Appendix A.4** of the revised version and illustrate the source of insight. In addition, we use experiments to verify the advantage of the cross-correlation coefficient over the cosine-similarity in GSCA architecture. Specifically, we conduct experiments on the ImageNet1k and Mini-ImageNet datasets using the dot product cosine-similarity instead of the cross-correlation coefficient in GSCA module, with the following results.

| Metohd | ImageNet-1k (Top-1) |Mini-ImageNet (Top-1)|
| :- |:-: | :-: |
|Baseline|77.28|80.55|
|Dot product cosine-similarity|75.69|80.32|
|Cross-correlation coefficient|78.08|81.59|

As shown in the above table, the cosine-similarity plays a poor role in GSCA. On the contrary, it reduces the performance of the baseline. It shows that using cosine-similarity in GSCA to evaluate the pairwise affinity between $Q$ and the vector $k$ generated by GAP is imperfect. Using the cross-correlation coefficient is a better choice.

**2. To your comment regarding Table4** “In the ImageNet-1k experiment part, authors does not demonstrate a significant improvement in top-1 accuracy when compared to other methods (Table 4).”

**Our responses** are: As shown in Table 4, the competitiveness of GSCA compared to other methods is that it achieves a better trade-off in accuracy-parameter and accuracy-inference speed. The superiority of GSCA is summarized as follows.

(1) As the baseline increases, the parameters added by the other methods increase, while GSCA remains parameter-free. For example, SENet and FcaNet add 2.5M, 4.7M and 6.5M parameters with ResNet 50 to 152.

(2) As baseline performance increases, GSCA's boosting effect also increases. For example, GSCA substantially outperformed SENet and ECANet in the resnet101 and 152 networks.

(3) GSCA achieves a better accuracy-inference speed trade-off. GSCA is faster and more accurate than SENet. GSCA achieves higher accuracy at an inference speed similar to ECANet. GSCA maintains a consistently faster inference speed than FcaNet, and the gap between GSCA-152 and FcaNet shrinks gradually (only a 0.03% difference between GSCA-152 and FcaNet).

(4) GSCA, as a spatial attention module, has good compatibility with other methods. For example, the combination of GSCA with SENet and ECANet further improves the accuracy of the original methods.

content.title: The Summary of Our Responses to All Official Reviews
content.comment:
Dear Reviewers, Area Chairs and Program Chairs,

We sincerely thank all three reviewers for their thorough and constructive comments, which made our paper more complete and clear.

In the past about ten days, we carefully improved the clarifications and the discussions of our work to address the concerns, the questions and the requests by all three reviewers. Summarily, we made the following improvements:

**(1)** To illustrate the role of cross-correlation coefficient in GSCA module (reviewer gy9w), we discuss the cross-correlation coefficient and the cosine-similarity in Appendix A.4 of the revised version and illustrate the source of insight. In addition, we conducted comparative experiments on ImageNet1k and Mini-ImageNet datasets. The results verify the advantage of the cross-correlation coefficient over the cosine-similarity in GSCA architecture.

**(2)** To better understand the function of the reverse operation (ahYw), we illustrate that the way k vector is generated causes GSCA to work differently than the self-attention intuition. Following the suggestion, we have visualized the GSCA module in the revised Appendix A.6 to intuitively illustrate the necessity of the reverse operation in the system.

**(3)** We respond to reviewers gy9w and 287a's concerns about the accuracy of the GSCA. The competitiveness of GSCA compared to other methods is that it achieves a better trade-off in accuracy-parameter and accuracy-inference speed. For different sizes of baselines, GSCA enhances baseline performance while consistently being parameter-free. As a spatial attention module, GSCA can be easily combined with channel attention to improve the original method. In downstream tasks, GSCA achieves equal or similar performance to SOTA with fewer parameters.

**(4)** We also provide detailed responses to the other concerns/questions raised by each reviewer one by one.

Finally, based on the constructive comments by all three reviewers and our responses, we carefully revised and updated the manuscript of our work. We hope our detailed responses and the updated manuscript are helpful to address the concerns and the questions of all reviewers.
